3:Frame Job brings captions in from a SubRip file, writes them from the speech in your clips, and writes a caption track back out as `.srt` or `.vtt`. Speech is recognised either **on this Mac**, with nothing uploaded, or by **AssemblyAI** in the cloud, using your own API key. Captions come out as two-line subtitles or as large word-by-word captions in one of five styles, where each word lights up as it is said. Every caption is an ordinary text clip, so it plays in the preview, burns into an export, and can be dragged, trimmed and restyled like any other clip.
21:- You can select a run of captions and restyle them together in the inspector's Clip tab, under **Text** ([Canvas and layers](canvas-and-layers.md)).
34:Choose **File ▸ Import Captions…** and pick a `.srt` file. The open panel reads "Choose a SubRip (.srt) caption file." and accepts `.srt` and any plain-text file, so a SubRip file saved as `.txt` imports too. A `.vtt` file is not read as WebVTT. Each cue becomes one text clip in the **Caption** preset, on a new track called **Captions** (or the next free number). The import is a single undo step, **Import Captions**.
42:- `<i>`, `<b>`, `<u>` and `<font>` tags and `{\an8}`-style overrides, which are removed, plus the common HTML entities (`&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, `'`, `'`, ` `)
80:| **Style** | **Subtitles** or one of the five word caption styles. See [Caption styles](#caption-styles). | The style you chose last time; Subtitles the first time. |
81:| *(looks)* | **Slide the pill**, **Fill words as spoken**, **Dim in pauses**. See [Looks](#looks-for-word-captions). | Each one as you last left it; off the first time. |
83:| **Replace** | "existing captions" swaps out earlier caption tracks over the same clips. See [Restyle a caption track](#restyle-a-caption-track). | Off |
115:**The transcript cache.** Each media file's transcript is kept in the project package and reused by the next run. A file whose cached transcript matches the request (same file, model, language, Speakers and Vocabulary) is not uploaded again and costs nothing. The caption style does not count, so restyling never uploads. A transcript made for Remove Filler Words also serves Generate Captions, so that file is not uploaded or billed again. The cache is kept per media entry, so two media entries over the same file are uploaded and billed separately. When no API key is set and every file in the run already has a current transcript, the hint changes to "Current cached transcripts will be used without an API key or network request." and **Generate** works without a key. With a key set, the usual hint stays, and the summary says there is nothing to upload. To force a fresh upload anyway, tick **Transcribe again**.
127:**Speakers.** With **Speakers** ticked, a change of speaker always starts a new cue or page. In the **Subtitles** style, each speaker's cues take their own colour, in the order the speakers first appear: white, yellow, cyan, green, then round again. Speakers are counted separately for each media file.
147:*Agents:* `transcribe`. It takes `clips` (the scope), `engine` (`apple`, the default, or `assemblyai`), `language` (`auto` by default with AssemblyAI), `style`, `replace`, `slide`, `fill`, `dim`, and, for AssemblyAI only, `speakers`, `vocabulary` and `refresh`, each refused by name without `engine: "assemblyai"`. It answers the cues in timeline ticks (with each word's timing for a word style) whether or not it places them, and `place: false` changes nothing at all. `replace` is refused with `subtitles` or with `place: false`; when it is given, a placed run lists the removed tracks' ids under `replaced`. The tool never remembers the sheet's engine, style or looks, and never downloads a language model. A language whose model is not installed is refused by name.
151:The **Subtitles** style makes classic two-line cues, built by these rules:
160:Each cue uses the **Caption** text preset: Source Sans 3 Regular at 3.5% of the canvas height, centred, on a 60% black backdrop, wrapping at 80% of the canvas width, with its box centred 38% of the frame height below the middle.
162:## Caption styles
164:The five word caption styles make the large, one-row captions used in shorts and reels. Instead of a cue, each clip holds a **page** of words with each word's timing, and the word being spoken is drawn the way the style says. All five are white with the spoken word marked. They are sized to the shorter side of the canvas, so a vertical and a horizontal canvas get the same text height.
166:| Style | Typeface | Case | How the spoken word shows | Position |
169:| **Highlight** | Montserrat Black, black outline | UPPERCASE | Turns yellow and pops to 112% | A quarter of the frame height below centre |
179:A page is filled to the width it actually measures in its style on your canvas, not to a word count:
184:- A single word too wide for the frame shrinks, down to 80% of the style's size, before it wraps.
190:The preview under the Style row shows a sample page drawn by the same renderer the canvas uses, at this canvas's proportions. It uses the first words of the first clip's cached transcript when there is one, and "This is how it looks" otherwise. A word style shows two frames, with the first word active and then the second. A ticked **Fill words as spoken** shows the fill half done, and a ticked **Slide the pill** shows the pill half-way through its slide. **Dim in pauses** is not previewed.
192:## Looks for word captions
194:Three checkboxes under the Style popup each add a look to a word style's pages. Each is off until you tick it, and the sheet remembers each one between runs. A box that does not apply to the chosen style is greyed out and does nothing, but keeps its tick for when you switch back.
196:| Look | What it does | Works with |
199:| **Fill words as spoken** | The word being said fills from left to right as it is spoken, taking at most 0.6 s. The part already said is in the highlight colour; the rest is in the upcoming colour (Karaoke's dimmed white), or not yet drawn in Build. | Highlight, Karaoke, Build |
200:| **Dim in pauses** | The page fades to half opacity during a pause of 0.25 s or more, then comes back before the next word. It also dims before the first word when that word starts late, and after the last word until the caption ends. Each fade takes 0.1 s. | All five word styles |
202:With **On this Mac** chosen and a word style selected, a note under the boxes reads "On-device words rarely carry a pause; this shows mostly with AssemblyAI." The on-device recogniser stretches each word's time across the silence after it, so few pauses are long enough to dim.
204:*Agents:* `transcribe`'s `slide`, `fill` and `dim`. Each is false unless given, never what the sheet last chose. `true` is refused by name with a style it would not show on, or with `place: false`; `false` is always accepted. A placed run given any of the three lists the looks that were on under `looks`.
206:## Restyle a caption track
208:A style is fixed when the captions are generated. To change it, generate again with **Replace** ticked:
211:2. Choose the new word style and looks.
217:**Replace** is live only for a word style, and only when there is a track it may replace. That means a track named **Captions** or **Captions N** that holds only text clips, each of which overlaps a clip being transcribed. Tracks outside the run's scope are left alone.
221:Captions are text clips, so the inspector's Clip tab edits them under **Text**: Content, Font, Style, Outline, Backdrop, Box, Reveal and Presets. Select several captions to change them together.
225:- **Case.** The style's capitals come from **Text ▸ Style ▸ UPPERCASE**. Untick it to show a page as written. Case is applied when the page is drawn, so the Content box shows the words as written, and changing case never drops the word timing.
226:- **Word style colours.** There is no inspector section for a page's word style (highlight colour, pop scale, pill colour). To change them, generate again with a different style, or have an agent use `set_text`'s `word_style`.
228:- **Reveal.** The text reveals (typewriter, word fade, line rise) do not apply to a timed page. The Reveal section says "Word style wins; the reveal does not apply."
231:*Agents:* `set_text` edits a caption like any text clip, including a page's `words` and `word_style`. When `words` is not empty, it must have exactly one timing for each word of the content. Otherwise the edit is refused: "this text is timed word by word: N timings for M words".
244:Nothing marks a track as a caption track, so any track made only of text clips can be exported, a titles track included. A word caption track is written one cue per page, with the page's words as written: the style's UPPERCASE, its word timings and its styling are not part of a `.srt` or `.vtt`.
275:- Word styles mark words by their timing only. There is no keyword emphasis and no emoji.
276:- A page's word style colours and scale cannot be edited in the inspector. Generate again, or have an agent use `set_text`'s `word_style`.
277:- Speaker colours apply only to the Subtitles style.
279:- A style cannot be switched on a placed track. Restyle by generating again with Replace.

# app/CLAUDE.md — Swift app rules

Applies to everything under `app/`. Build/verification commands and the FFI
lockstep are in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the full design is
`designs/spec/` (§3–4 the UI, §7.4–7.8 the platform side; its `README.md` is
the index). The
long form of each entry below — why each file is the shape it is, and the
traps its history turned up — is `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` (the
full history, every size toll and measurement, is archived; see its
"Original" line); this file is what governs a file now. Files
are listed by family; a file with a header comment of its own carries its
detail there.

## File map

**The core's edge.**
- `ReelCore.swift` — the **only** home for `rc_*` calls: `ReelProject`
  (handle + lazily decoded `ProjectSnapshot`; `json`, `snapshot` and
  `planJSON` are memoised PER HANDLE, so keep handles rather than minting
  them; so is `sourceMap(_:)`, `rc_project_source_map` decoded and checked
  once per handle and clip, SR-20), timecode, snapping (export presets/sizes/settings are
  `ExportValues.swift`'s, a pure move, HDR H-1), `ReelSpeed.limits` (the
  core's speed range and audio ceiling, typed as `SpeedLimits` in
  `CoreValues.swift` — no Swift file types a speed bound), `ReelColor` (`rc_normalise_color`, G-25), `ReelGraphicPackage` (`rc_graphic_package_write`, G-46; `read`, `rc_graphic_package_read`, G-47), `GraphicLibrary.usage()` (`rc_graphic_library_usage`) and
  `ReelContainer` (`rc_container_*`, a WebM/Matroska file's index,
  #216-R) and `ReelWebM` (`rc_webm_*`, the `av1_webm` writer, spec §11 CX-15) and `ReelHDR10` (`rc_hdr10_peak`, spec §11 HD-6; `av1Peak`,
  `rc_hdr10_av1_peak`, HD-18; `stillPeak`, `rc_hdr10_still_peak`, HD-20), and `GraphicLibrary.imageCache(limit:)`
  (`rc_graphic_image_cache`, G-39); `ReelCoreError`, `Fps.ffiPair` and `ReelTime`'s
  seconds conversions are `CoreValues.swift`'s (G6 phase 5's toll T2 and speed ramps SR4-0,
  pure moves); the typed patches are `TypedPatches.swift`'s (`VideoPatch`,
  `AudioPatch`, `ClipPatch`, the `ActionPatch` extension; a pure move, B73),
  `TextPatch` (with `case`, `words` and `word_style`) is `TextPatch.swift`'s,
  moved out so it could grow, and `ShapePatch` `ShapePatch.swift`'s (a pure
  move, the toll for `ReelColor`). `VideoPatch.color` is a sparse `ColorPatch`
  (`GradeProps.swift`, which holds `ColorAdjust` (moved out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading-2 G2-0) with its neutrality helpers, and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(tone:)`, and the wheels' `ColorWheel`, `ColorWheels`,
  `ColorWheelPatch`, `ColorWheelsPatch`, `ColorWheelKind` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(wheels:)` (GR-11)); `VideoPatch.curves` is
  `CurveProps.swift`'s `ColorCurvesPatch`, beside `CurvePoint`,
  `CurveDomain`, `CurveChannel`, `CurveBlend` (a channel blended inside an
  action, spec §11 GR-34; `ColorCurves.blends`, never encoded), `ColorCurves` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(curves:)` (GR-12, the hue curves GR-32; a
  pure move out of `GradeProps.swift`, grading-4 T4-0); `VideoPatch.qualifier` is
  `QualifierProps.swift`'s `ColorQualifierPatch`, beside `ColorQualifier` (its
  `blur`, `blursSelection` and `selectionSigma`, GR-35), `QualifierUniforms`
  (`blurred`, set only by `drawAdjustment`) and the pick's `QualifierSample`
  (GR-13), so a row writes
  only its own key to every selected clip. `word_style` has ONE
  app-side writer, `CaptionLayout.place` (W-10). `ReelAgentSocket` (road map
  14's MC2) wraps `rc_agent_socket_start` / `_release`: `start` throws the
  core's sentence, `release` is the quit's unlink-if-still-ours with no join.
  The `dictionary` extensions on the property types are
  `OpDictionaries.swift`'s (below).
  The graphics engine's wrappers are here too: `GraphicLibrary` (`addFont`,
  `addAsset`, `rasterize`, `families()`; frozen by its first compile,
  rasterize or `families()`) and
  `GraphicModule` (`compile`, `describeJSON`, `svg`; it holds its library
  strongly); their values `GraphicDiagnostic` (with `.error`, `.noModule`
  and `.of(_:)`, the one spelling of a diagnostic made from a message, a
  missing module or a thrown error), `GraphicFailure` (what a
  `diag_out` failure throws; `err_out` stays `ReelCoreError`) and
  `GraphicRaster` are `CoreValues.swift`'s, with `GraphicUsage`, the byte
  bridges `withByteBuffer` and `withMutableByteBuffer` (G-46's toll; never
  `UnsafeMutablePointer(mutating:)`), `SpeedLimits` (a pure move,
  clean-up batch 2), `ReelCoreError` and `Fps.ffiPair` (G6 phase 5's toll), and
  `CoreJSON` (`value`, `snapTicks`: `clipState`'s and `snapCandidates`' JSON
  halves, clean-up round 3's toll; `array`, `overrides`, C1's tolls; `ExportSize.list`,
  `ExportSettings.decoded`, `ReelAV1.Config.decoded`, `withNonNullBytes`, codec-export C5's
  toll), and C1's
  fix-pass moves: `ReelAV1.Config` / `.Color` (an extension of `ReelCore.swift`'s
  `ReelAV1`, whose `rc_av1_*` calls stay there), `GraphicDiagnostic.list(json:)`,
  `GraphicFailure.checkSides`, `SpeedLimits.decoded` and the free `withBytes`.
  `MediaDescriptor`, `MediaOriginal`, `mediaURL(for:)`, `originalURL(for:)`,
  `revealURL(for:)` (the original, else the copy), `isTrashed` and
  `bookmarkString(for:)` are `MediaDescriptor.swift`'s: a `media[]` element
  minus its id, and the media-file resolvers; they call no `rc_*`.
  It is also where the op table is read BACK: `ReelOp.coreNames()` over
  `rc_op_names`, and `ReelOp.coreSchemas()` over `rc_op_schemas` — every
  op's ARGUMENTS as JSON Schema, keyed by op name, which
  `AgentCatalog.opTool` prints for all sixty-four op tools.
  `deinit` frees the Rust allocation. It also holds **the one read of
  `rc_project_apply`'s TWO message channels**, in the header's own order — a
  sentence is a refusal, an error message is invalid input, neither written
  is an identity — answered as the `ReelEdit` below.
- `OpDictionaries.swift` — the `dictionary` extensions on the §5.2
  property types (`CropInsets` … `Gradient`), the model's own key names; a
  pure move out of `ReelCore.swift` (#190, issue batch B52b; road map 14's
  MC2 made the same move as `PropsDictionaries.swift`, and the merge kept
  main's file). With
  `ReelCore.swift` and `ReelOps.swift`, the only files that write an op
  argument. `putNullable` is the one writer of a three-state (`T??`)
  patch key: absent, an explicit null, or the value.
- `ReelOps.swift` — `OpArgs`, `ReelOp` and one typed factory per row of
  `core/src/edit.rs`'s op table, plus a RAW factory beside the typed one at
  each door that takes a CALLER's own object — ELEVEN of them (`setVideoRaw`,
  `setAudioRaw`, `setTextRaw`, `setShapeRaw`, `setClipRaw`,
  `setActionEndRaw`, `addTextClipRaw`, `addShapeClipRaw`, `setCanvasRaw`,
  `addBackgroundRaw`, `addZoomActionRaw`), which takes the
  caller's own object as `Any` — never `[String: Any]`, so a non-object is
  refused by the CORE in the words that name the group — and forwards it;
  there is no untyped op-JSON call site anywhere else. Where only ONE
  argument is the caller's (a colour, a region, a new clip's patch) the typed
  factory DELEGATES to the raw one, mapping its optional explicitly, because
  an `Optional<T>.none` widened to `Any?` is a non-nil `Any` wrapping a nil.
  The typed `setActionEnd` LIFTS every top-level null out of its patch into
  `off` (spec §11 CI-14: a typed `.some(nil)` is a switch turned OFF, kept
  at the end), and a null slot inside `audio.eq` into `audio.eq.<slot>`
  (AU-88); `setActionEndRaw`'s nulls stay removals, which is what
  `clearOps` and every agent call send, and it writes `off` only when non-empty and `schema` only when non-nil
  (the agent door fills it for a graphic end from the module's current
  revision, spec §11 G-34).
  `addZoomActionRaw`'s region is `Any` and not `Any?`: an absent key and an
  explicit null are opposite intentions there, and only the tool can tell
  them apart.
  `scope` is a member folded into `json`; `documentLevelNames` MIRRORS
  `scope.rs`'s `refused_inside` (eight names) so one edit can mix a
  document-level op with scoped ones. A table, with
  `edit.rs`'s size exemption.
- `ReelOpSchema.swift` — what an op TAKES, mirroring what
  `core/src/op_schema.rs` publishes: the `properties` and `required` of one
  op's arguments, which are the two things `AgentServer.tool` takes, and
  `table(from:)`, which reads `rc_op_schemas`' JSON into them (SR4-0's pure
  move out of `ReelCore.swift`, whose `coreSchemas()` keeps the call). Here
  rather than next door for `ReelEdit.swift`'s reason — it names no `rc_*`
  symbol — and `properties` stays `[String: Any]` because a Swift type per
  kind would be another spelling of the table.
- `ReelEdit.swift` — what an op ANSWERS, mirroring `core/src/outcome.rs`:
  `ReelEdit` (`.applied` / `.identity` / `.refused`), `ReelRefusal` (the op
  the core declined and the rule's own sentence, carried verbatim), and the
  fold that applies a LIST — which names no `rc_*` symbol, so it lives here
  and not next door. **Only `.applied` is an undo step**; the other two are
  both "the project did not change" and differ only in what a caller can
  SAY. `.project` is the spelling for a caller that treats a refusal as
  nothing happened (a probe, a live drag), and there is one on
  `ReelEdit?` too for the `try?` probes. In the fold **a refusal does not
  stop the list** — a later op still runs after one, exactly as after an
  identity — and the FIRST refusal is answered only when nothing applied.
- `ProjectSnapshot.swift` · `TextProps.swift` · `MotionProps.swift` ·
  `WordProps.swift` · `MediaSnapshot.swift` · `ActionSnapshot.swift` · `ShapeProps.swift` · `CompositionPlan.swift` · `GradeProps.swift` · `CurveProps.swift` · `AudioProps.swift` — the `Codable`, READ-ONLY mirror
  of spec §5.2 every view draws from. READ-ONLY means never written back as
  is: the stored properties are `var`, so a writer edits a COPY
  (`var s = current(); s.blur = v`) rather than rebuilding one through the
  defaulted memberwise initialiser, which silently drops a field it does not
  spell out; `MotionProps.with(_:)` is motion's per-slot copy (#357). `CompositionPlan.swift` (a pure move out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading GR1) is the plan's Swift side (spec §7.2): `PlanSegment`,
  `PlanRamp`, `PlanTrack`, `PlanInstruction` and `CompositionPlan`; `PlanSpeedRamp.source` is
  its `map` as a `SourceMap`, checked once at decode and not a coding key (SR-20 (c)); `PlanDuck`
  and `ducks` are a speech ducker's own multiplier (format 29, spec §11 AU-113). `AudioProps.swift`
  (a pure move out of `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, road map "audio" AP11's toll) holds the audio group:
  `AudioProps`, `DuckProps` and `CompressorProps`, with format 29's `DuckMode`,
  `DuckProps.mode` / `preRoll` / `hold` and `FadeShape` (and the popups' titles), and format
  30's `LimiterProps` (`audio.limiter`, spec §11 AU-21) with its patch body,
  and format 31's `AudioProps.isolation` (AU-50), and format 32's `eq`, `hum` and `channels`

**Frozen files.** `EditorViewController.swift`, `TimelineView.swift`,
`PreviewCanvasView.swift`, `AgentServer.swift` are **frozen at current
size**: anything adding more than ~50 lines goes in an extension file
(`EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift`, `TimelineView+<Feature>.swift`,
`AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`) or a new `…SheetController`, and the frozen
file keeps only the wiring — a stored property, a closure assignment, a
validator arm, a draw call. The pieces extension files build on are therefore
internal, not private. Pitfalls: a selector declared `@objc` on an extension
needs NO forward in the frozen file (a second declaration is an error); a
command whose body sits at the foot of a non-extension feature file carries
its validator arm there too, or the item falls through to the closing
`return true`; `handleEditorCharacter`'s bare-key `switch` matches in SOURCE
order, so a bare `case "x"` goes BELOW any modified `case "x" where …`; and
`handleEditorKey` refuses while a sheet is attached, because a sheet is
window-modal and the preview panel's forwarded keys would otherwise reach
the key map behind it.

- `Playback.swift` (+`Meter`, +`PreviewQuality`, +`Step`, +`Scope`, +`Prefetch`) — one
  `AVPlayer` over the plan's composition; the transport, JKL, the rate KVO; `+Meter` is the level meter, moved out under
  the size rule; `+Scope` also holds `seekFinished()` and `report(_:)`
  (hdr H-3's pure move). `recompose()` re-colours the player's copy of the
  composition without a rebuild (`previewComposition(…, sdrVersion:)`, the
  way Preview Quality does): View ▸ Show SDR Version, spec §11 HD-14. **Only a seek someone ASKED for reports a time**:
  `seek(to:)` is that door, and Playback's own RESTORES — the rebuild's item
  swap and re-seek, the paused refresh's round trip — go through `startSeek`
  silently and report once, only if they come to rest off the last reported
  tick; a scope change seeks through `seekAfterRebuild(to:)`: its time is the
  NEW container's, so the outgoing item is neither sought nor heard and the
  rebuild in flight lands there, heard once (#130, `scope_playhead_probe.py`);
  an asked seek that arrives while a restore is seeking is heard once, when it
  lands; `update`'s same-plan and empty-plan arms discard a rebuild in flight;
  a held scope change whose rebuild fails, or whose new plan is empty, drops
  the item rather than leave the outgoing one, keeps its time and is heard
  once (`endHoldWithoutItem` in `+Scope`, #185; the seek flags are internal
  for `+Scope` alone); `rebuildHop` is the probe's seam, nil in the app, and
  its block takes an error it delivers as the build's failure; `report(_:)` is the one
  caller of `onTimeChanged`. While paused, an observer callback is heard only
  for the tick the player is at or seeking to, and only when it differs from
  the last report — a late callback for a superseded seek or a swapped-out
  item is dropped (#204, #209; `playhead_echo_probe.py` twice·1, pause·1) —
  and every seek's landing reports its rest once when it differs. `+Step`
  also holds the main hop `onMain`. `+Prefetch` is the playing preview's
  graphics prefetch (spec §11 G-36, #127): `syncPrefetch(from:seeking:)`,
  called from the rate KVO, `startSeek` (with the seek's TARGET, never
  `currentTime`, which still reads the player there) and `update`'s
  same-plan arm while playing, and stopped in `invalidate` and `deinit`;
  `recipeKey` is internal for it. `syncPrefetch` first notes activity for
  Background render, and `startBackgroundRender` (G-38) starts a paused pass
  on the composition's grid (`prefetchGrid`), answering why not
  (`.busy` re-arms the clock, `.notNeeded` waits for the next activity). An echoed restore
  moved the playhead (0 and back on every rebuild), and the timeline reveals
  every moved playhead, so a clip drag yanked the view
  (`playhead_echo_probe.py`). **A paused refresh is a one-tick round trip**
  (`refreshPausedFrame`): a zero-tolerance seek to the current time is a
  NO-OP on macOS 26.5.1, so the refresh seeks one tick off and returns; parked
  at the end it rests on the last frame's final tick, because the end tick
  composes black. Do not put a same-time seek back. Preview Quality overrides
  `renderSize` on a copy of the builder's
  `BuiltComposition.videoConfiguration` here (`Playback.previewComposition`,
  static so `phase8_chrome.py` calls it), keeping the
  canvas's EXACT aspect (`m · (w/g, h/g)`, coarser when the divisor does not
  divide `g`, Full for a coprime canvas); `AVPlayerItem.videoComposition` is
  a COPY property, so the setter re-assigns. `makePreviewLayer` is the one
  door to a second `AVPlayerLayer`.
  The item is dropped only for an EMPTY timeline (`plan.duration <= 0`,
  where the transport beeps). Never gate it on the plan's track lists: a
  timeline of only graphics, text, shapes or images has no plan track and
  plays over the builder's placeholder (road map 10 §10.8,
  `media_less_playback_probe.py`).

# app/CLAUDE.md — Swift app rules

Applies to everything under `app/`. Build/verification commands and the FFI
lockstep are in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the full design is
`designs/spec/` (§3–4 the UI, §7.4–7.8 the platform side; its `README.md` is
the index). The
long form of each entry below — why each file is the shape it is, and the
traps its history turned up — is `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` (the
full history, every size toll and measurement, is archived; see its
"Original" line); this file is what governs a file now. Files
are listed by family; a file with a header comment of its own carries its
detail there.

## File map

**The core's edge.**
- `ReelCore.swift` — the **only** home for `rc_*` calls: `ReelProject`
  (handle + lazily decoded `ProjectSnapshot`; `json`, `snapshot` and
  `planJSON` are memoised PER HANDLE, so keep handles rather than minting
  them; so is `sourceMap(_:)`, `rc_project_source_map` decoded and checked
  once per handle and clip, SR-20), timecode, snapping (export presets/sizes/settings are
  `ExportValues.swift`'s, a pure move, HDR H-1), `ReelSpeed.limits` (the
  core's speed range and audio ceiling, typed as `SpeedLimits` in
  `CoreValues.swift` — no Swift file types a speed bound), `ReelColor` (`rc_normalise_color`, G-25), `ReelGraphicPackage` (`rc_graphic_package_write`, G-46; `read`, `rc_graphic_package_read`, G-47), `GraphicLibrary.usage()` (`rc_graphic_library_usage`) and
  `ReelContainer` (`rc_container_*`, a WebM/Matroska file's index,
  #216-R) and `ReelWebM` (`rc_webm_*`, the `av1_webm` writer, spec §11 CX-15) and `ReelHDR10` (`rc_hdr10_peak`, spec §11 HD-6; `av1Peak`,
  `rc_hdr10_av1_peak`, HD-18; `stillPeak`, `rc_hdr10_still_peak`, HD-20), and `GraphicLibrary.imageCache(limit:)`
  (`rc_graphic_image_cache`, G-39); `ReelCoreError`, `Fps.ffiPair` and `ReelTime`'s
  seconds conversions are `CoreValues.swift`'s (G6 phase 5's toll T2 and speed ramps SR4-0,
  pure moves); the typed patches are `TypedPatches.swift`'s (`VideoPatch`,
  `AudioPatch`, `ClipPatch`, the `ActionPatch` extension; a pure move, B73),
  `TextPatch` (with `case`, `words` and `word_style`) is `TextPatch.swift`'s,
  moved out so it could grow, and `ShapePatch` `ShapePatch.swift`'s (a pure
  move, the toll for `ReelColor`). `VideoPatch.color` is a sparse `ColorPatch`
  (`GradeProps.swift`, which holds `ColorAdjust` (moved out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading-2 G2-0) with its neutrality helpers, and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(tone:)`, and the wheels' `ColorWheel`, `ColorWheels`,
  `ColorWheelPatch`, `ColorWheelsPatch`, `ColorWheelKind` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(wheels:)` (GR-11)); `VideoPatch.curves` is
  `CurveProps.swift`'s `ColorCurvesPatch`, beside `CurvePoint`,
  `CurveDomain`, `CurveChannel`, `CurveBlend` (a channel blended inside an
  action, spec §11 GR-34; `ColorCurves.blends`, never encoded), `ColorCurves` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(curves:)` (GR-12, the hue curves GR-32; a
  pure move out of `GradeProps.swift`, grading-4 T4-0); `VideoPatch.qualifier` is
  `QualifierProps.swift`'s `ColorQualifierPatch`, beside `ColorQualifier` (its
  `blur`, `blursSelection` and `selectionSigma`, GR-35), `QualifierUniforms`
  (`blurred`, set only by `drawAdjustment`) and the pick's `QualifierSample`
  (GR-13), so a row writes
  only its own key to every selected clip. `word_style` has ONE
  app-side writer, `CaptionLayout.place` (W-10). `ReelAgentSocket` (road map
  14's MC2) wraps `rc_agent_socket_start` / `_release`: `start` throws the
  core's sentence, `release` is the quit's unlink-if-still-ours with no join.
  The `dictionary` extensions on the property types are
  `OpDictionaries.swift`'s (below).
  The graphics engine's wrappers are here too: `GraphicLibrary` (`addFont`,
  `addAsset`, `rasterize`, `families()`; frozen by its first compile,
  rasterize or `families()`) and
  `GraphicModule` (`compile`, `describeJSON`, `svg`; it holds its library
  strongly); their values `GraphicDiagnostic` (with `.error`, `.noModule`
  and `.of(_:)`, the one spelling of a diagnostic made from a message, a
  missing module or a thrown error), `GraphicFailure` (what a
  `diag_out` failure throws; `err_out` stays `ReelCoreError`) and
  `GraphicRaster` are `CoreValues.swift`'s, with `GraphicUsage`, the byte
  bridges `withByteBuffer` and `withMutableByteBuffer` (G-46's toll; never
  `UnsafeMutablePointer(mutating:)`), `SpeedLimits` (a pure move,
  clean-up batch 2), `ReelCoreError` and `Fps.ffiPair` (G6 phase 5's toll), and
  `CoreJSON` (`value`, `snapTicks`: `clipState`'s and `snapCandidates`' JSON
  halves, clean-up round 3's toll; `array`, `overrides`, C1's tolls; `ExportSize.list`,
  `ExportSettings.decoded`, `ReelAV1.Config.decoded`, `withNonNullBytes`, codec-export C5's
  toll), and C1's
  fix-pass moves: `ReelAV1.Config` / `.Color` (an extension of `ReelCore.swift`'s
  `ReelAV1`, whose `rc_av1_*` calls stay there), `GraphicDiagnostic.list(json:)`,
  `GraphicFailure.checkSides`, `SpeedLimits.decoded` and the free `withBytes`.
  `MediaDescriptor`, `MediaOriginal`, `mediaURL(for:)`, `originalURL(for:)`,
  `revealURL(for:)` (the original, else the copy), `isTrashed` and
  `bookmarkString(for:)` are `MediaDescriptor.swift`'s: a `media[]` element
  minus its id, and the media-file resolvers; they call no `rc_*`.
  It is also where the op table is read BACK: `ReelOp.coreNames()` over
  `rc_op_names`, and `ReelOp.coreSchemas()` over `rc_op_schemas` — every
  op's ARGUMENTS as JSON Schema, keyed by op name, which
  `AgentCatalog.opTool` prints for all sixty-four op tools.
  `deinit` frees the Rust allocation. It also holds **the one read of
  `rc_project_apply`'s TWO message channels**, in the header's own order — a
  sentence is a refusal, an error message is invalid input, neither written
  is an identity — answered as the `ReelEdit` below.
- `OpDictionaries.swift` — the `dictionary` extensions on the §5.2
  property types (`CropInsets` … `Gradient`), the model's own key names; a
  pure move out of `ReelCore.swift` (#190, issue batch B52b; road map 14's
  MC2 made the same move as `PropsDictionaries.swift`, and the merge kept
  main's file). With
  `ReelCore.swift` and `ReelOps.swift`, the only files that write an op
  argument. `putNullable` is the one writer of a three-state (`T??`)
  patch key: absent, an explicit null, or the value.
- `ReelOps.swift` — `OpArgs`, `ReelOp` and one typed factory per row of
  `core/src/edit.rs`'s op table, plus a RAW factory beside the typed one at
  each door that takes a CALLER's own object — ELEVEN of them (`setVideoRaw`,
  `setAudioRaw`, `setTextRaw`, `setShapeRaw`, `setClipRaw`,
  `setActionEndRaw`, `addTextClipRaw`, `addShapeClipRaw`, `setCanvasRaw`,
  `addBackgroundRaw`, `addZoomActionRaw`), which takes the
  caller's own object as `Any` — never `[String: Any]`, so a non-object is
  refused by the CORE in the words that name the group — and forwards it;
  there is no untyped op-JSON call site anywhere else. Where only ONE
  argument is the caller's (a colour, a region, a new clip's patch) the typed
  factory DELEGATES to the raw one, mapping its optional explicitly, because
  an `Optional<T>.none` widened to `Any?` is a non-nil `Any` wrapping a nil.
  The typed `setActionEnd` LIFTS every top-level null out of its patch into
  `off` (spec §11 CI-14: a typed `.some(nil)` is a switch turned OFF, kept
  at the end), and a null slot inside `audio.eq` into `audio.eq.<slot>`
  (AU-88); `setActionEndRaw`'s nulls stay removals, which is what
  `clearOps` and every agent call send, and it writes `off` only when non-empty and `schema` only when non-nil
  (the agent door fills it for a graphic end from the module's current
  revision, spec §11 G-34).
  `addZoomActionRaw`'s region is `Any` and not `Any?`: an absent key and an
  explicit null are opposite intentions there, and only the tool can tell
  them apart.
  `scope` is a member folded into `json`; `documentLevelNames` MIRRORS
  `scope.rs`'s `refused_inside` (eight names) so one edit can mix a
  document-level op with scoped ones. A table, with
  `edit.rs`'s size exemption.
- `ReelOpSchema.swift` — what an op TAKES, mirroring what
  `core/src/op_schema.rs` publishes: the `properties` and `required` of one
  op's arguments, which are the two things `AgentServer.tool` takes, and
  `table(from:)`, which reads `rc_op_schemas`' JSON into them (SR4-0's pure
  move out of `ReelCore.swift`, whose `coreSchemas()` keeps the call). Here
  rather than next door for `ReelEdit.swift`'s reason — it names no `rc_*`
  symbol — and `properties` stays `[String: Any]` because a Swift type per
  kind would be another spelling of the table.
- `ReelEdit.swift` — what an op ANSWERS, mirroring `core/src/outcome.rs`:
  `ReelEdit` (`.applied` / `.identity` / `.refused`), `ReelRefusal` (the op
  the core declined and the rule's own sentence, carried verbatim), and the
  fold that applies a LIST — which names no `rc_*` symbol, so it lives here
  and not next door. **Only `.applied` is an undo step**; the other two are
  both "the project did not change" and differ only in what a caller can
  SAY. `.project` is the spelling for a caller that treats a refusal as
  nothing happened (a probe, a live drag), and there is one on
  `ReelEdit?` too for the `try?` probes. In the fold **a refusal does not
  stop the list** — a later op still runs after one, exactly as after an
  identity — and the FIRST refusal is answered only when nothing applied.
- `ProjectSnapshot.swift` · `TextProps.swift` · `MotionProps.swift` ·
  `WordProps.swift` · `MediaSnapshot.swift` · `ActionSnapshot.swift` · `ShapeProps.swift` · `CompositionPlan.swift` · `GradeProps.swift` · `CurveProps.swift` · `AudioProps.swift` — the `Codable`, READ-ONLY mirror
  of spec §5.2 every view draws from. READ-ONLY means never written back as
  is: the stored properties are `var`, so a writer edits a COPY
  (`var s = current(); s.blur = v`) rather than rebuilding one through the
  defaulted memberwise initialiser, which silently drops a field it does not
  spell out; `MotionProps.with(_:)` is motion's per-slot copy (#357). `CompositionPlan.swift` (a pure move out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading GR1) is the plan's Swift side (spec §7.2): `PlanSegment`,
  `PlanRamp`, `PlanTrack`, `PlanInstruction` and `CompositionPlan`; `PlanSpeedRamp.source` is
  its `map` as a `SourceMap`, checked once at decode and not a coding key (SR-20 (c)); `PlanDuck`
  and `ducks` are a speech ducker's own multiplier (format 29, spec §11 AU-113). `AudioProps.swift`
  (a pure move out of `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, road map "audio" AP11's toll) holds the audio group:
  `AudioProps`, `DuckProps` and `CompressorProps`, with format 29's `DuckMode`,
  `DuckProps.mode` / `preRoll` / `hold` and `FadeShape` (and the popups' titles), and format
  30's `LimiterProps` (`audio.limiter`, spec §11 AU-21) with its patch body,
  and format 31's `AudioProps.isolation` (AU-50), and format 32's `eq`, `hum` and `channels`
  (`AudioEQProps.swift`, AU-31, AU-33, AU-34), and format 33's `gate` and `deEsser`
  (`AudioDynamicsProps.swift`, AU-43, AU-45), and format 34's `voice`
  (`VoiceProps.swift`, AU-140), and format 37's `leveller`
  (`AudioDynamicsProps.swift`, AU-66);
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`'s `TransitionSnapshot.audioShape` is `plus_3db` when absent, and
  `MediaSnapshot.speech` the media's saved spans. `ShapeProps.swift` (a pure
  move out of `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading L3) holds the shape group: `StrokeProps`,
  `GradientStop`, `Gradient` and `ShapeProps`. `GradeProps.swift` holds `ColorAdjust` (a pure move out of `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading-2 G2-0) beside grading's other value types. `ActionSnapshot.swift` (a pure move out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, B87) holds `ActionPatch`, `ActionSnapshot` and `ActionGraphicPatch` — an
  end's `graphic.props` and `kinds`, whose `dictionary` sends `props` only. `MediaSnapshot` (a pure move out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`) carries a copy's or an ffmpeg conversion's `original`, and its `name` is
  the one display-name spelling: the original's name when one is recorded. **Its enums decode LENIENTLY**
  — a misspelt kind becomes the first case, a `T??` field a clear — which is
  why a caller-authored object is never decoded through them (below). The
  one exception is `ClipSource`: an unknown `source.kind` THROWS, and
  `ReelProject.snapshot` then falls back to `.empty`, so the WHOLE project
  draws empty with no error. A new source kind in the core is therefore a
  `ClipSource` case in the same phase (road map 10's G2a added `graphic`): no
  agent handler reads a caller-authored OBJECT at all. A scalar enum
  argument is a different thing and several handlers still parse one by name
  (`enumArg` for `add_zoom_action`'s `fit` or an action's `curve`,
  `set_transition`'s `kind` by hand): the
  core refuses those too, and what this rule forbids is decoding a caller's
  object through a lenient type.
  `MotionProps.dictionary` always writes all three keys, `NSNull` for a nil
  slot, because a core patch of `motion` deep-merges — it is the
  APP's writer saying all three slots, not a replace rule, and it is the only
  edge that writes a whole motion. `MotionEdge` also supplies nonpersisted
  zero-duration activity and inactive display/menu titles (E2-27).
  `TextProps.swift` is the text group and `RecipeReveal` (with format version
  9's `textCase` / `words` / `wordStyle`, the recipe's `word` / `wordPop` and,
  since format version 12, `wordGlide` / `wordFill` / `wordDim`), a pure move
  out of `ProjectSnapshot.swift` because a stored property cannot be added
  from an extension. `RecipeReveal` reads and writes its OWN keys — siblings of
  `hash` and `text` in the `text` source — through `init(siblingsOf:)` and
  `encodeSiblings(to:)`, so a new recipe key costs `FrameRecipe.swift`
  nothing; a key spelled other than the snake-case converter spells it
  decodes silently to that key's default (the amount to 1, the rest to nil).
  `ProjectSnapshot+Graphic.swift` mirrors
  `model_graphic.rs`'s `GraphicProps` as `GraphicSnapshot` (`in` is
  `sourceIn`) and `GraphicPropValue` (string, number, bool; anything else
  `.null`), decoded into `ClipSnapshot.graphic`; `props` keys keep the
  module's own spelling (snake-case conversion does not reach a dictionary's
  keys). `WordProps.swift` mirrors `model_words.rs`
  (`TextCase`, `TextWord`, `WordMode`, `ActivePill`, `WordStyle`)
  — `WordStyle.dictionary` writes ALL eight keys (`active_fill` and `pause_dim` since format version 12; `ActivePill.dictionary` writes `glide`), `NSNull` for a nil slot,
  `MotionProps.dictionary`'s rule, because the core deep-merges
  `word_style` — and holds
  what the renderer and the inspector share: `laidContent` (`case` applied —
  every layout and string index is in ITS UTF-16 space, never `content`'s),
  `tokenCount`, `isUntimedPage`, `TextPatch.contentEdit` and
  `InspectorBinding.contentOps` / `ops(textContent:)` — the Content write,
  decided PER CLIP: `words: []` beside the content in one `set_text` only for
  base clips whose count changed, and never `words` in an action end (W-2,
  W-6). It lives there, not in `InspectorPane.swift`, for the size rule.

**The document.**
- `ProjectDocument.swift` (+`DisplayStem`, +`Recording`, +`SelectedAction`, +`Import`, +`Graphics`, +`GraphicFiles`, +`UndoGroup`, +`CacheSaves`, +`Alerts`)
  — NSDocument, `.framejob` package read/write, and the single mutation
  point (see Undo); `applyEdit`'s `.refused` arm beeps and then posts
  `projectDocumentDidRefuse` with the `ReelRefusal` (spec §11 CI-10), which
  the editor forwards to the inspector's refusal strip. Holds the SIX pieces of view state nothing persists —
  playhead, clip selection, in/out range, `selectedMedia`, `nestPath` and
  `selectedAction` — re-clamped by `clampViewState` in that order with the
  scope FIRST, since the selection clamp measures against whatever
  container the scope left. `selectedAction` (spec §11 CI-1) is nil or one
  action of the SINGLE selected clip; `+SelectedAction` holds its queries,
  its one deliberate writer `selectAction(_:)` (which stores nil for an id
  that is not `singleSelectedClip`'s) and the ENTRY rule

size**: anything adding more than ~50 lines goes in an extension file

validator arm, a draw call. The pieces extension files build on are therefore

command whose body sits at the foot of a non-extension feature file carries

3:Frame Job brings captions in from a SubRip file, writes them from the speech in your clips, and writes a caption track back out as `.srt` or `.vtt`. Speech is recognised either **on this Mac**, with nothing uploaded, or by **AssemblyAI** in the cloud, using your own API key. Captions come out as two-line subtitles or as large word-by-word captions in one of five styles, where each word lights up as it is said. Every caption is an ordinary text clip, so it plays in the preview, burns into an export, and can be dragged, trimmed and restyled like any other clip.
21:- You can select a run of captions and restyle them together in the inspector's Clip tab, under **Text** ([Canvas and layers](canvas-and-layers.md)).
34:Choose **File ▸ Import Captions…** and pick a `.srt` file. The open panel reads "Choose a SubRip (.srt) caption file." and accepts `.srt` and any plain-text file, so a SubRip file saved as `.txt` imports too. A `.vtt` file is not read as WebVTT. Each cue becomes one text clip in the **Caption** preset, on a new track called **Captions** (or the next free number). The import is a single undo step, **Import Captions**.
42:- `<i>`, `<b>`, `<u>` and `<font>` tags and `{\an8}`-style overrides, which are removed, plus the common HTML entities (`&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, `'`, `'`, ` `)
80:| **Style** | **Subtitles** or one of the five word caption styles. See [Caption styles](#caption-styles). | The style you chose last time; Subtitles the first time. |
81:| *(looks)* | **Slide the pill**, **Fill words as spoken**, **Dim in pauses**. See [Looks](#looks-for-word-captions). | Each one as you last left it; off the first time. |
83:| **Replace** | "existing captions" swaps out earlier caption tracks over the same clips. See [Restyle a caption track](#restyle-a-caption-track). | Off |
115:**The transcript cache.** Each media file's transcript is kept in the project package and reused by the next run. A file whose cached transcript matches the request (same file, model, language, Speakers and Vocabulary) is not uploaded again and costs nothing. The caption style does not count, so restyling never uploads. A transcript made for Remove Filler Words also serves Generate Captions, so that file is not uploaded or billed again. The cache is kept per media entry, so two media entries over the same file are uploaded and billed separately. When no API key is set and every file in the run already has a current transcript, the hint changes to "Current cached transcripts will be used without an API key or network request." and **Generate** works without a key. With a key set, the usual hint stays, and the summary says there is nothing to upload. To force a fresh upload anyway, tick **Transcribe again**.
127:**Speakers.** With **Speakers** ticked, a change of speaker always starts a new cue or page. In the **Subtitles** style, each speaker's cues take their own colour, in the order the speakers first appear: white, yellow, cyan, green, then round again. Speakers are counted separately for each media file.
147:*Agents:* `transcribe`. It takes `clips` (the scope), `engine` (`apple`, the default, or `assemblyai`), `language` (`auto` by default with AssemblyAI), `style`, `replace`, `slide`, `fill`, `dim`, and, for AssemblyAI only, `speakers`, `vocabulary` and `refresh`, each refused by name without `engine: "assemblyai"`. It answers the cues in timeline ticks (with each word's timing for a word style) whether or not it places them, and `place: false` changes nothing at all. `replace` is refused with `subtitles` or with `place: false`; when it is given, a placed run lists the removed tracks' ids under `replaced`. The tool never remembers the sheet's engine, style or looks, and never downloads a language model. A language whose model is not installed is refused by name.
151:The **Subtitles** style makes classic two-line cues, built by these rules:
160:Each cue uses the **Caption** text preset: Source Sans 3 Regular at 3.5% of the canvas height, centred, on a 60% black backdrop, wrapping at 80% of the canvas width, with its box centred 38% of the frame height below the middle.
162:## Caption styles
164:The five word caption styles make the large, one-row captions used in shorts and reels. Instead of a cue, each clip holds a **page** of words with each word's timing, and the word being spoken is drawn the way the style says. All five are white with the spoken word marked. They are sized to the shorter side of the canvas, so a vertical and a horizontal canvas get the same text height.
166:| Style | Typeface | Case | How the spoken word shows | Position |
169:| **Highlight** | Montserrat Black, black outline | UPPERCASE | Turns yellow and pops to 112% | A quarter of the frame height below centre |
179:A page is filled to the width it actually measures in its style on your canvas, not to a word count:
184:- A single word too wide for the frame shrinks, down to 80% of the style's size, before it wraps.
190:The preview under the Style row shows a sample page drawn by the same renderer the canvas uses, at this canvas's proportions. It uses the first words of the first clip's cached transcript when there is one, and "This is how it looks" otherwise. A word style shows two frames, with the first word active and then the second. A ticked **Fill words as spoken** shows the fill half done, and a ticked **Slide the pill** shows the pill half-way through its slide. **Dim in pauses** is not previewed.
192:## Looks for word captions
194:Three checkboxes under the Style popup each add a look to a word style's pages. Each is off until you tick it, and the sheet remembers each one between runs. A box that does not apply to the chosen style is greyed out and does nothing, but keeps its tick for when you switch back.
196:| Look | What it does | Works with |
199:| **Fill words as spoken** | The word being said fills from left to right as it is spoken, taking at most 0.6 s. The part already said is in the highlight colour; the rest is in the upcoming colour (Karaoke's dimmed white), or not yet drawn in Build. | Highlight, Karaoke, Build |
200:| **Dim in pauses** | The page fades to half opacity during a pause of 0.25 s or more, then comes back before the next word. It also dims before the first word when that word starts late, and after the last word until the caption ends. Each fade takes 0.1 s. | All five word styles |
202:With **On this Mac** chosen and a word style selected, a note under the boxes reads "On-device words rarely carry a pause; this shows mostly with AssemblyAI." The on-device recogniser stretches each word's time across the silence after it, so few pauses are long enough to dim.
204:*Agents:* `transcribe`'s `slide`, `fill` and `dim`. Each is false unless given, never what the sheet last chose. `true` is refused by name with a style it would not show on, or with `place: false`; `false` is always accepted. A placed run given any of the three lists the looks that were on under `looks`.
206:## Restyle a caption track
208:A style is fixed when the captions are generated. To change it, generate again with **Replace** ticked:
211:2. Choose the new word style and looks.
217:**Replace** is live only for a word style, and only when there is a track it may replace. That means a track named **Captions** or **Captions N** that holds only text clips, each of which overlaps a clip being transcribed. Tracks outside the run's scope are left alone.
221:Captions are text clips, so the inspector's Clip tab edits them under **Text**: Content, Font, Style, Outline, Backdrop, Box, Reveal and Presets. Select several captions to change them together.
225:- **Case.** The style's capitals come from **Text ▸ Style ▸ UPPERCASE**. Untick it to show a page as written. Case is applied when the page is drawn, so the Content box shows the words as written, and changing case never drops the word timing.
226:- **Word style colours.** There is no inspector section for a page's word style (highlight colour, pop scale, pill colour). To change them, generate again with a different style, or have an agent use `set_text`'s `word_style`.
228:- **Reveal.** The text reveals (typewriter, word fade, line rise) do not apply to a timed page. The Reveal section says "Word style wins; the reveal does not apply."
231:*Agents:* `set_text` edits a caption like any text clip, including a page's `words` and `word_style`. When `words` is not empty, it must have exactly one timing for each word of the content. Otherwise the edit is refused: "this text is timed word by word: N timings for M words".
244:Nothing marks a track as a caption track, so any track made only of text clips can be exported, a titles track included. A word caption track is written one cue per page, with the page's words as written: the style's UPPERCASE, its word timings and its styling are not part of a `.srt` or `.vtt`.
275:- Word styles mark words by their timing only. There is no keyword emphasis and no emoji.
276:- A page's word style colours and scale cannot be edited in the inspector. Generate again, or have an agent use `set_text`'s `word_style`.
277:- Speaker colours apply only to the Subtitles style.
279:- A style cannot be switched on a placed track. Restyle by generating again with Replace.

# app/CLAUDE.md — Swift app rules

Applies to everything under `app/`. Build/verification commands and the FFI
lockstep are in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the full design is
`designs/spec/` (§3–4 the UI, §7.4–7.8 the platform side; its `README.md` is
the index). The
long form of each entry below — why each file is the shape it is, and the
traps its history turned up — is `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` (the
full history, every size toll and measurement, is archived; see its
"Original" line); this file is what governs a file now. Files
are listed by family; a file with a header comment of its own carries its
detail there.

## File map

**The core's edge.**
- `ReelCore.swift` — the **only** home for `rc_*` calls: `ReelProject`
  (handle + lazily decoded `ProjectSnapshot`; `json`, `snapshot` and
  `planJSON` are memoised PER HANDLE, so keep handles rather than minting
  them; so is `sourceMap(_:)`, `rc_project_source_map` decoded and checked
  once per handle and clip, SR-20), timecode, snapping (export presets/sizes/settings are
  `ExportValues.swift`'s, a pure move, HDR H-1), `ReelSpeed.limits` (the
  core's speed range and audio ceiling, typed as `SpeedLimits` in
  `CoreValues.swift` — no Swift file types a speed bound), `ReelColor` (`rc_normalise_color`, G-25), `ReelGraphicPackage` (`rc_graphic_package_write`, G-46; `read`, `rc_graphic_package_read`, G-47), `GraphicLibrary.usage()` (`rc_graphic_library_usage`) and
  `ReelContainer` (`rc_container_*`, a WebM/Matroska file's index,
  #216-R) and `ReelWebM` (`rc_webm_*`, the `av1_webm` writer, spec §11 CX-15) and `ReelHDR10` (`rc_hdr10_peak`, spec §11 HD-6; `av1Peak`,
  `rc_hdr10_av1_peak`, HD-18; `stillPeak`, `rc_hdr10_still_peak`, HD-20), and `GraphicLibrary.imageCache(limit:)`
  (`rc_graphic_image_cache`, G-39); `ReelCoreError`, `Fps.ffiPair` and `ReelTime`'s
  seconds conversions are `CoreValues.swift`'s (G6 phase 5's toll T2 and speed ramps SR4-0,
  pure moves); the typed patches are `TypedPatches.swift`'s (`VideoPatch`,
  `AudioPatch`, `ClipPatch`, the `ActionPatch` extension; a pure move, B73),
  `TextPatch` (with `case`, `words` and `word_style`) is `TextPatch.swift`'s,
  moved out so it could grow, and `ShapePatch` `ShapePatch.swift`'s (a pure
  move, the toll for `ReelColor`). `VideoPatch.color` is a sparse `ColorPatch`
  (`GradeProps.swift`, which holds `ColorAdjust` (moved out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading-2 G2-0) with its neutrality helpers, and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(tone:)`, and the wheels' `ColorWheel`, `ColorWheels`,
  `ColorWheelPatch`, `ColorWheelsPatch`, `ColorWheelKind` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(wheels:)` (GR-11)); `VideoPatch.curves` is

  pure move out of `GradeProps.swift`, grading-4 T4-0); `VideoPatch.qualifier` is
  `QualifierProps.swift`'s `ColorQualifierPatch`, beside `ColorQualifier` (its

  (GR-13), so a row writes

  core's sentence, `release` is the quit's unlink-if-still-ours with no join.

  `OpDictionaries.swift`'s (below).

  `MediaDescriptor`, `MediaOriginal`, `mediaURL(for:)`, `originalURL(for:)`,

  `bookmarkString(for:)` are `MediaDescriptor.swift`'s: a `media[]` element

  `AgentCatalog.opTool` prints for all sixty-four op tools.
  `deinit` frees the Rust allocation. It also holds **the one read of
  `rc_project_apply`'s TWO message channels**, in the header's own order — a
  sentence is a refusal, an error message is invalid input, neither written
  is an identity — answered as the `ReelEdit` below.
- `OpDictionaries.swift` — the `dictionary` extensions on the §5.2

- `ReelOps.swift` — `OpArgs`, `ReelOp` and one typed factory per row of

  `setActionEndRaw`, `addTextClipRaw`, `addShapeClipRaw`, `setCanvasRaw`,

  revision, spec §11 G-34).

  explicit null are opposite intentions there, and only the tool can tell
  them apart.
  `scope` is a member folded into `json`; `documentLevelNames` MIRRORS

- `ReelOpSchema.swift` — what an op TAKES, mirroring what
  `core/src/op_schema.rs` publishes: the `properties` and `required` of one
  op's arguments, which are the two things `AgentServer.tool` takes, and

- `ReelEdit.swift` — what an op ANSWERS, mirroring `core/src/outcome.rs`:
  `ReelEdit` (`.applied` / `.identity` / `.refused`), `ReelRefusal` (the op

  fold that applies a LIST — which names no `rc_*` symbol, so it lives here
  and not next door. **Only `.applied` is an undo step**; the other two are
  both "the project did not change" and differ only in what a caller can

  nothing happened (a probe, a live drag), and there is one on
  `ReelEdit?` too for the `try?` probes. In the fold **a refusal does not
  stop the list** — a later op still runs after one, exactly as after an

- `ProjectSnapshot.swift` · `TextProps.swift` · `MotionProps.swift` ·
  `WordProps.swift` · `MediaSnapshot.swift` · `ActionSnapshot.swift` · `ShapeProps.swift` · `CompositionPlan.swift` · `GradeProps.swift` · `CurveProps.swift` · `AudioProps.swift` — the `Codable`, READ-ONLY mirror
  of spec §5.2 every view draws from. READ-ONLY means never written back as
  is: the stored properties are `var`, so a writer edits a COPY

  end's `graphic.props` and `kinds`, whose `dictionary` sends `props` only. `MediaSnapshot` (a pure move out of

  the one display-name spelling: the original's name when one is recorded. **Its enums decode LENIENTLY**

  why a caller-authored object is never decoded through them (below). The
  one exception is `ClipSource`: an unknown `source.kind` THROWS, and

  `ClipSource` case in the same phase (road map 10's G2a added `graphic`): no
  agent handler reads a caller-authored OBJECT at all. A scalar enum

  (`enumArg` for `add_zoom_action`'s `fit` or an action's `curve`,
  `set_transition`'s `kind` by hand): the

  object through a lenient type.

**Frozen files.** `EditorViewController.swift`, `TimelineView.swift`,
`PreviewCanvasView.swift`, `AgentServer.swift` are **frozen at current
size**: anything adding more than ~50 lines goes in an extension file
(`EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift`, `TimelineView+<Feature>.swift`,
`AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`) or a new `…SheetController`, and the frozen
file keeps only the wiring — a stored property, a closure assignment, a
validator arm, a draw call. The pieces extension files build on are therefore
internal, not private. Pitfalls: a selector declared `@objc` on an extension
needs NO forward in the frozen file (a second declaration is an error); a
command whose body sits at the foot of a non-extension feature file carries
its validator arm there too, or the item falls through to the closing
`return true`; `handleEditorCharacter`'s bare-key `switch` matches in SOURCE
order, so a bare `case "x"` goes BELOW any modified `case "x" where …`; and
`handleEditorKey` refuses while a sheet is attached, because a sheet is
window-modal and the preview panel's forwarded keys would otherwise reach
the key map behind it.

  `AVPlayer` over the plan's composition; the transport, JKL, the rate KVO; `+Meter` is the level meter, moved out under
  the size rule; `+Scope` also holds `seekFinished()` and `report(_:)`
  (hdr H-3's pure move). `recompose()` re-colours the player's copy of the
  composition without a rebuild (`previewComposition(…, sdrVersion:)`, the
  way Preview Quality does): View ▸ Show SDR Version, spec §11 HD-14. **Only a seek someone ASKED for reports a time**:
  `seek(to:)` is that door, and Playback's own RESTORES — the rebuild's item
  swap and re-seek, the paused refresh's round trip — go through `startSeek`
  silently and report once, only if they come to rest off the last reported
  tick; a scope change seeks through `seekAfterRebuild(to:)`: its time is the
  NEW container's, so the outgoing item is neither sought nor heard and the
  rebuild in flight lands there, heard once (#130, `scope_playhead_probe.py`);
  an asked seek that arrives while a restore is seeking is heard once, when it
  lands; `update`'s same-plan and empty-plan arms discard a rebuild in flight;
  a held scope change whose rebuild fails, or whose new plan is empty, drops
  the item rather than leave the outgoing one, keeps its time and is heard
  once (`endHoldWithoutItem` in `+Scope`, #185; the seek flags are internal
  for `+Scope` alone); `rebuildHop` is the probe's seam, nil in the app, and
  its block takes an error it delivers as the build's failure; `report(_:)` is the one
  caller of `onTimeChanged`. While paused, an observer callback is heard only
  for the tick the player is at or seeking to, and only when it differs from
  the last report — a late callback for a superseded seek or a swapped-out
  item is dropped (#204, #209; `playhead_echo_probe.py` twice·1, pause·1) —
  and every seek's landing reports its rest once when it differs. `+Step`
  also holds the main hop `onMain`. `+Prefetch` is the playing preview's
  graphics prefetch (spec §11 G-36, #127): `syncPrefetch(from:seeking:)`,
  called from the rate KVO, `startSeek` (with the seek's TARGET, never
  `currentTime`, which still reads the player there) and `update`'s
  same-plan arm while playing, and stopped in `invalidate` and `deinit`;
  `recipeKey` is internal for it. `syncPrefetch` first notes activity for
  Background render, and `startBackgroundRender` (G-38) starts a paused pass
  on the composition's grid (`prefetchGrid`), answering why not
  (`.busy` re-arms the clock, `.notNeeded` waits for the next activity). An echoed restore
  moved the playhead (0 and back on every rebuild), and the timeline reveals
  every moved playhead, so a clip drag yanked the view
  (`playhead_echo_probe.py`). **A paused refresh is a one-tick round trip**
  (`refreshPausedFrame`): a zero-tolerance seek to the current time is a
  NO-OP on macOS 26.5.1, so the refresh seeks one tick off and returns; parked
  at the end it rests on the last frame's final tick, because the end tick
  composes black. Do not put a same-time seek back. Preview Quality overrides

  divide `g`, Full for a coprime canvas); `AVPlayerItem.videoComposition` is
  a COPY property, so the setter re-assigns. `makePreviewLayer` is the one
  door to a second `AVPlayerLayer`.

  timeline of only graphics, text, shapes or images has no plan track and

docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md:3:Frame Job has two commands for cleaning up a spoken recording such as a screencast, a tutorial or a talking-head take. **Remove Silences** finds the dead air and cuts it. **Remove Filler Words** finds the ums and uhs and cuts them on the words' own timings. Both show what they would cut before they cut anything, and both make the whole cut as one undo step. An agent can read the same answers, and it can read a clip's transcript to cut false starts.
docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md:29:- A gap with nothing audible in it is left alone. Remove Silences takes dead air out of a recording; it does not close the gaps you placed between clips. **Clip ▸ Close Gap** does that.
docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md:38:| Voice | Nobody is talking. An on-device voice-activity model listens to each media file once and keeps its answer with the project. A quiet microphone isn't mistaken for silence, and a hum isn't mistaken for speech. | Yes |
docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md:68:- **Nests.** "Quiet inside a nest is left alone… Open the nest (⌘↓) and remove its silences there to take the dead air out." This appears when a nest held enough quiet to have been cut.
docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md:70:*Agents:* `detect_silence` answers the same ranges the sheet would cut and changes nothing. It takes `clips` (the Selected clips scope; leave it out to use the sheet's opening rule), `mode` (`voice` or `level`), `voice_confidence` (0.1–0.9, default 0.5, Voice mode only), `threshold_db` (at or below 0), and `min_length` and `padding` (in ticks, 600,000 per second). Pass its `ranges` to `ripple_delete_ranges` to make the cut. It also answers `count`, `removes` (ticks), `scope` (`selected` or `audible`), `clips`, `mode`, `judged_by_level_clips`, `voice_pending`, `proposed_by_mix_clips` when the mix alone makes a waiting clip quiet, and `protected_nests` (the nest clips a quiet run crossed, left uncut; open one with `set_scope` and call again to look for dead air inside it). Files still being analysed are listed under `pending_peaks`; call again shortly. `voice_confidence` is refused in Level mode, and `mode: "voice"` is refused when the voice model can't be used.
docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md:125:*Agents:* `detect_fillers` answers the ranges the sheet would cut and changes nothing. It takes `clips` and lists each kept run under `fillers`, each left-in run under `dropped` with its reason, files with no filler transcript under `needs_transcript`, and locked clips under `locked`. It also answers `count`, `removes`, `scope` and `clips`, plus `skipped` when `clips` is given (each named clip it couldn't read, with the reason). Pass its `ranges` to `ripple_delete_ranges`. `transcribe_for_fillers` (`media`) is the Transcribe button: a paid upload that answers `ready` when `detect_fillers` can read that file. On a media that already has a filler transcript it uploads nothing and answers `ready: true`; otherwise it answers `uploaded`, `cached`, `audio_seconds`, `engine` and `language`. It is refused with no AssemblyAI key and for a media no clip plays. The built-in assistant can't use it.
docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md:131:- **Where the words come from.** The file's saved AssemblyAI transcript when it has a current one. Otherwise this Mac's own speech recogniser runs over the clip, which takes a few seconds per minute of speech. Reading a transcript never uses the network and never uploads anything.
docs/guide/cleanup-tools.md:149:It cuts false starts only when you ask. It can also remove fillers the same way **Remove Filler Words** does, and take out silences the way **Remove Silences** does (`detect_silence`, then one `ripple_delete_ranges`). Any cut an agent makes this way, whether silences, fillers or false starts, is one undo step labelled **Undo Ripple Delete**, not the sheet's name. The assistant can't start a paid filler transcription: press **Transcribe** in the sheet yourself. See [The assistant](assistant.md).

**Premiere (Object Mask):** Adobe's AI Object Mask shipped in the Creative Cloud 26.0 update, which also dropped the "Pro" name. It was previewed last October at Adobe MAX as a beta tool. Hovering over a subject and clicking once builds a mask that tracks the object through the scene. It uses a new Adobe AI model that runs entirely on-device. Tracking is up to 20 times faster than the previous version, and live tracking previews are included. Early beta users reported issues, such as some of the object masks are offline and will be ignored when exporting through Media Encoder, and a beta forum reply noted that variable refresh rate videos have problems with object mask tracking, and converting to a constant frame rate tracks much better.

**Final Cut Pro (Magnetic Mask):** Magnetic Mask arrived with Final Cut Pro 11. It works very similarly to Photoshop's "Select and Mask", but for video. Apple's documentation says you can use the Magnetic Mask to easily isolate people, objects, and shapes from the background using machine learning. Final Cut Pro can then track the item's movement in the clip using machine learning and apply the mask to each frame automatically. One reviewer reported rendering at around 70% realtime (UHD footage at 25 frames per second) on an M2 Max MacBook Pro.

**Comparison:** Both tools use AI to select and track subjects, but they were released in different ways. Premiere's Object Mask came out of beta with the Premiere 26 update in January 2026. Final Cut's Magnetic Mask was part of the Final Cut Pro 11 launch, and one reviewer said it has leaped over the quality of tracking currently available in other NLEs. That is one reviewer's opinion, not a head-to-head test.

The search turned up mostly third-party tutorials and community write-ups, not Apple's official documentation, so treat the details as unverified against Apple's docs.

- **Pipeline:** One write-up describes the chain as mic input via AVAudioEngine's tap, then AVAudioConverter, then AnalyzerInput, with a SpeechAnalyzer coordinating a SpeechTranscriber . Audio goes in as AnalyzerInput, and results come out of an AsyncSequence.
- **Format conversion:** A common trap is skipping conversion. One author warns that code can compile and still produce no text if it follows the WWDC sample without handling the mic wiring correctly. The fix shown is converting each buffer to the format SpeechAnalyzer asked for before yielding it.
- **Volatile results:** Volatile results are enabled through the transcriber's reporting options. One example passes .volatileResults, and an alternative is the .progressiveLiveTranscription preset, which skips timestamps. Adding .audioTimeRange as an attribute option gives per-word timing.
- **Finalizing:** To turn pending volatile text into final text when stopping, one guide says to call finalizeAndFinishThroughEndOfInput on the analyzer. Another stops the audio engine, removes the tap, and finalizes to get remaining volatile results as finalized.
- **Models:** One source notes that the language model downloads on first use, so the model should be checked before live capture starts.
- **Latency:** One developer reports time to the first volatile result of about 0.3–0.5s on a warm start on an iPhone 16e running iOS 26.5.

The most detailed working example is a community sample repo (MIT licensed) at github.com/simplememofast/ios26-speechanalyzer-live-mic, which is worth checking against Apple's WWDC26 sample code and the SpeechAnalyzer documentation before relying on it.

**The 25% figure and its history:** The 25%+ number is the later one. Dubbing also takes real investment, since creators must supply their own tracks (multi-language audio lets you upload your own dubbed audio tracks), and YouTube recommends that those tracks match the primary language translation as closely as possible.

# init(installedSource:target:)

Creates a translation session to translate between a given source and target language already installed on device.

```
convenience init(installedSource source: Locale.Language, target: Locale.Language?)
```

## Discussion

If one or both of the languages aren’t installed on the device already, attempting to translate will throw errors. In order to get the person’s permission to download
languages that aren’t already installed, translate using a [`TranslationSession`](/documentation/Translation/TranslationSession) provided by <doc://com.apple.documentation/documentation/SwiftUI/View/translationTask(_:action:)> or
<doc://com.apple.documentation/documentation/SwiftUI/View/translationTask(source:target:action:)>.

> Note: If you created a `TranslationSession` using ``doc://com.apple.Translation/documentation/Translation/TranslationSession/init(installedSource:target:)``, you don’t need a `.translationTask()`; however, you will need a ``doc://com.apple.Translation/documentation/Translation/TranslationSession/sourceLanguage``.

**Submagic emoji and keyword highlight captions**

- Submagic's emoji and highlight features are AI-driven. Its marketing describes auto emojis and keyword highlights as a way to emphasize key points in your content.

The feature lets you change the primary caption color and add up to three highlight colors for emphasizing specific words. The help center also notes that not all Submagic themes support word highlighting.

The search turned up good coverage of DaVinci Resolve's IntelliScript but no evidence of a native Premiere Pro feature that builds a timeline from a script.

**DaVinci Resolve (IntelliScript):** Resolve's IntelliScript takes your written script, transcribes your footage, and matches spoken lines to scripted lines. It then builds a rough cut in script order using the best-matching takes, and places alternatives on extra tracks for review (added IntelliScript, which matches transcribed takes against a script and assembles a timeline of the best takes). It's described as a Studio feature, costing $295; transcription and transcript editing are available in the free version. Users have also reported that IntelliScript is not always reliable. One forum poster concluded that Intelliscript is an unworkable solution for my needs at this time for rough-cutting multiple videos. Another found the feature sometimes failed to build a timeline, though the first two lines did cut correctly.

**Premiere Pro:** Premiere has text-based editing, and both Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve allow you to insert clips from the transcription window. A 2026 Adobe Community thread shows an editor asking for a way to import a text paper edit so Premiere will automatically splice in the paper edit script directly onto a sequence, which suggests this isn't native. The same thread mentions a third-party tool, Sheetscut, that generates an FCP XML file that you can import directly into Premiere from a word-level transcript and a paper edit.

**Caveat:** I ran one search and didn't check Adobe's own documentation, so Premiere's current capabilities may have changed. Verify the Premiere answer against Adobe's release notes before relying on it.
